column2: When a thousand divine women danced for you, for many years of pleasure, as you blazed with fortune,
all wearing lotus garlands, all shining like gold: what was your mind then, and what is it now, lord of the Danavas?
You had a great golden parasol adorned with gems, where the gandharvas danced, seven thousand in seven groups.
You had a great sacrificial post, wholly of gold, as you conquered, where you gave away tens of thousands of thousands of cows.
When you, sacrificing, went around the whole earth by the throw of the staff according to rule, what was then in your heart?
I do not see your golden pitcher, your parasol or your fan; and I do not see the garland Brahma gave you, lord of the asuras."
[Bali said:] "You do not see my pitcher, parasol or fan, nor will you see the garland Brahma gave me, Vasava.
You ask me about my jewels hidden in a cave; when my time comes, then you will see them.
This is not fitting for your fame or your family, that one of full fortune should boast to one without fortune.
The wise, who have trained wisdom, are satisfied with knowledge, patient and good, neither grieve in sorrows nor rejoice in prosperity.
You, Purandara, boast with a common mind; when you become as I am, you will not speak so."
[Shakra said:] "When you went, surrounded by kinsmen in thousands of vehicles, scorching all the worlds, disregarding us,
seeing now this very wretched condition of yours in strength, abandoned by kinsmen and friends, do you grieve or not?
Seeing this fall, after the incomparable love and the worlds that once stood in your power, do you grieve or not?"
[Bali said:] "Seeing this impermanence in the turning of my own time, Shakra, I do not grieve, for all this has an end.
These bodies of beings have an end, lord of the immortals; therefore, Shakra, I do not grieve; this is not from any fault of mine.
Life and body are born together after death; both grow together; both perish together.
Having thus come, helpless, to this state alone, if I know it so, what pain is there for me who know?
The death of beings is their end, as the ocean is of rivers; men who do not rightly know this are bewildered, wielder of the thunderbolt.
In gaining understanding a man drives away all sin; freed from sin, he gains goodness and, abiding in goodness, grows serene.
But those who turn back from it, or are born again and again, wretched, suffer, driven by misfortunes.
Success in affairs and misfortune, life and death, and the fruit of pleasure and pain, I neither hate nor desire.
The man who kills anyone kills one already killed; neither of them knows, he who kills and he who is killed.
Whoever, Maghavan, having killed and conquered, acts the man is in fact not the doer; the doer is another who does it.
Both the rise and the destruction of the world are made by him; what is done is done by what is done, and the doer has another still.
Earth, wind, space, water and fire as fifth: beings have these as their source; what lament is there in that?
One of great learning or little, the strong or the weak, the handsome or ugly, the fortunate or unfortunate,
Time takes all, deep, by its own splendour; when I have come under Time's sway, what pain is there for me who know?
It burns the burnt, strikes the struck, and destroys the destroyed first; a man obtains what is to be obtained.
It has no island, no far shore, no near shore is seen; I do not see its end, thinking of the divine ordinance.
If Time did not destroy beings as I look on, I would have joy, pride and anger, lord of Shachi.
Knowing me as an eater of chaff living in a lonely house, bearing an ass's form, you revile me, pointing to it.
If I wished I could take many forms of myself, seeing which, terrifying, you would flee from me.
Time takes all, Time gives all; all is upheld by Time; do not make a show of manliness, Shakra.
Formerly all trembled when I was angry, Purandara; yet I know the eternal dharma of this world, Shakra.
You too should look at it so; do not fall into wonder at yourself; origin and power never rest in oneself.
Your mind is as childish today as it was before; look, Maghavan, and gain a final understanding.
Gods, men, ancestors, gandharvas, serpents and rakshasas were all in my power; you know all that, Vasava.
Honour to that quarter where Bali, son of Virochana, is, so they approached me, bewildered by the envy of mind.
I do not grieve over that, nor over my fall, lord of Shachi; this is my settled understanding: I stand in the power of the ruler.
One born in a good family, handsome and mighty, is seen living in sorrow with his ministers; it must be so.
One of bad family, a fool, ill-born, Shakra, is seen living happily with ministers; it must be so.
A good woman, endowed with beauty, is seen unfortunate, Shakra; one without marks and ugly is seen fortunate.
This was not made by us, Shakra, nor made by you, wielder of the thunderbolt, that you are as you are or that we are as we are.
It is not your deed nor others'; how is it mine, Shatakratu, whether prosperity or not? It is made by turn.
I see you shining, standing as king of the gods, glorious, radiant, and roaring over me.
If it were not so, and Time did not stand overpowering me, I would strike you down today with my fist, with your own garland.
But this is not the time for valour; the time for forbearance has come; Time sets up everything and Time cooks it.
If Time has come upon me, a mighty lord of the Danavas, roaring and burning, whom else will it not come to?
By one of you the radiances of all twelve great-souled Adityas have been taken from me, king of the gods.
I alone bear the waters and release them, Vasava; I warm the three worlds, and I flash.
I guard, plunder, give and take; I restrain and rule in the worlds, the lord and master.
Today that lordship of mine has turned back, lord of the immortals; plunged in the army of Time, all that does not appear to me.
I am not the doer, nor you, nor another is the doer, lord of Shachi; the worlds are enjoyed in turn, Shakra, by chance.
The Vedic scholars say it has months and half-months as its house, covered with days and nights, the seasons as doors, the year as its face.
Some people, by intelligence, say all this is to be thought on; I shall go through this thought in five ways, fivefold.
Brahman is deep, impenetrable, great, like an ocean of water; they call it without beginning or end, imperishable and supreme.
Placing a mark in beings, they hold that it is without mark, those men who see the truth, as certainly this.
He thinks of the reversal of beings, "he has gone"; this is not all to be gone to, for beyond nature there is something.
Where will you go, not having gone to the goal of all beings? He is not to be left by one who runs, nor lost by one who stands; all the senses do not see him in five ways.
Some call him fire, some Prajapati; the season, month, half-month, days and moments.
Forenoon, afternoon, and others say midday, and also a moment; though one, he is spoken of in many ways. Know that to be Time, in whose power is all this.
Many thousands of Indras have passed away, Vasava, endowed with strength and valour, just as you are, lord of Shachi.
You too, Shakra, mighty king of the gods, proud of strength, when the time comes, mighty Time will quell.
He who takes all this: therefore be steady, Shakra; he cannot be passed by me, you or those before.
The royal fortune supreme which you gain and think is established in me is false; she does not stay in one place.
She has stood with thousands of Indras more excellent than you; and fickle, leaving me, she has come to you, lord of the wise.
Do not do so again, Shakra; you ought to be calm; leaving you too, in such a state, she will quickly go to another."
Seeing her shining with radiance, the blessed Shakra, Vasava, his eyes wide with astonishment, asked Bali:
Bali, who is this going out, shining, crested, who stood with you, with armlets, shining by her own splendour?
[Bali said:] "I know her neither as asuric, divine nor human; ask her yourself, or do as you please, Vasava."
[Shakra said:] "Who are you, who have gone out from Bali, shining, crested? Tell me, who do not know, your name, fair-smiling one.
Who are you, standing like illusion, shining by your own splendour, having left the lord of the Daityas, fair-browed? Tell me that truly."
[Shri said:] "Virochana did not know me, nor Bali, Virochana's son; they call me Duhsaha and Vidhitsa.
They call me Bhuti, Lakshmi, and Shri, Vasava; you, Shakra, do not know me; none of the gods know me."
[Shakra said:] "Why do you do this for me, or for Bali, that you, long a dweller, leave him, Duhsaha?"
[Shri said:] "He was always devoted to brahmanas, truthful, master of his senses; but he came to envy brahmanas, and touched ghee while impure.
Formerly devoted to sacrifice, this fool said to the worlds, 'Sacrifice to me alone,' and was overcome by Time.
So, Shakra, driven out, I shall dwell in you, Vasava; I must be borne with care, with austerity and valour."
[Shakra said:] "Is there among gods, men or all beings a man who alone could bear you, lotus-dwelling one?"
[Shri said:] "Neither god, gandharva, asura nor rakshasa, none, Purandara, is able to bear me alone."
[Shakra said:] "Dwell in me ever, auspicious one; tell me how; I shall do your word; you ought to speak truth."
[Shri said:] "I shall stay always in you, lord of the gods, as you wish; learn how: divide me fourfold by the rule seen in the Veda."
[Shakra said:] "I shall place you as I am able, by my strength; but let there be no fault in me, with Lakshmi ever near.
The earth among men is the bearer of beings and their source; may she bear a quarter of you; so I think, and she can."
[Shri said:] "This quarter of mine is laid down, the one established on the earth; now, Shakra, lay down well my second quarter."
[Shakra said:] "Waters among men, flowing, are servants; may they bear your quarter; the waters are enough to bear it."
[Shri said:] "This quarter of mine is laid down, the one established in waters; now, Shakra, lay down well my third quarter."
[Shakra said:] "In whom the gods and sacrifices are founded, in whom the Vedas are established, fire will bear your third quarter well."
[Shri said:] "This quarter of mine is laid down, the one established in fire; now, Shakra, lay down well my fourth quarter."
[Shakra said:] "The good among men who are devoted to brahmanas and truthful: may they bear your quarter; the good are enough to bear it."
[Shri said:] "This quarter of mine is laid down, the one established in the good; thus laid down, Shakra, set me down among beings."
[Shakra said:] "Whoever among beings here harms you, whom I have thus laid down, he will be hateful to me; so hear my word."
[Bhishma said:] Then, abandoned by Shri, the king of the Daityas, Bali, said: "As long as the sun burns in front, so far the south.
So far the west, and likewise the north; and when the sun at midday goes to its setting, then again there will be a war of gods and asuras, and I shall conquer you.
When the sun will warm all the worlds standing in one place, then in the battle of gods and asuras I shall conquer you, Shatakratu."
[Shakra said:] "I have been commanded by Brahma, 'You are not to be killed'; therefore, Bali, I do not hurl the thunderbolt at your head.
Go as you wish, lord of the Daityas; good luck to you, great asura. The sun never burns standing in the middle.
His rule was set long ago by the Self-born; he goes unceasingly, warming the subjects by truth.
His course is six months north and south, by which the sun goes in the worlds, giving cold and heat."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed by Indra, the Daitya lord Bali, Bharata, went to the southern quarter, while Purandara went to the north.
Hearing this word sung by Bali, called the word of non-ego, the thousand-eyed Indra then ascended to the sky.
Deprived of fortune, sitting like an unshaken ocean, knowing the arising and passing of beings, Purandara said to him:
Bound by snares, fallen from your place, come under the power of foes, deprived of fortune, Namuchi, do you grieve or not?
[Namuchi said:] "The body is tormented by grief and nothing is gained; enemies rejoice; there is no help in grief.
Therefore, Shakra, I do not grieve, for all this has an end; from torment beauty and dharma fall away, lord of the gods.
Having put aside that sorrow born of dejection that has come, one should meditate in the mind on what is delightful and good, knowing it.
In whatever way a man sets his mind on the good, in just that way all his purposes become clear; there is no doubt.
There is one ruler, there is no second ruler; the ruler rules the man lying in the womb. Instructed by him, as water flows down a slope, as I am appointed, so I carry on.
Knowing being and non-being, the heavier, I know the better, but I do not do it; doing good to friends in their hopes of dharma, as I am appointed, so I carry on.
Sages, gods, great asuras, the old knowers of the three Vedas and sages in the forest: what calamities do not come upon them in the world? But those who know high and low are not confused.
The wise man is not angry, not attached, neither despondent nor exultant; he does not grieve in hardship or calamity of wealth, abiding by nature like the immovable Himalaya.
He whom the highest success of wealth does not gladden, and whom calamity in its time does not bewilder, who serves pleasure and pain and the middle alike, that man is a bearer of the yoke.
In whatever state a man comes to be, he should take delight in it, untroubled; thus he should drive away the grown torment, born of the mind, that makes the body weary.

He who, having come into that hall, that assembly, among assembly-sitters, has no fear of the assembly, the wise man who plunges into the truth of dharma and goes forward, that man is a bearer of the yoke.

The deeds of the wise are hard to follow; the wise are not bewildered at a time of bewilderment; if Gautama, though fallen from his place, was not bewildered, so the old man, having come to a hard calamity.
Not by mantras, strength, valour, wisdom or manliness does a mortal gain what is not to be gained; what lament is there?
What the Creators ordained long ago for one so born, that I shall undergo; what will death do to me?
One gains only what is to be gained, goes only where he is to go, obtains only what is to be obtained, pains and pleasures.
The man who, knowing this wholly, is not bewildered, skilled in pleasure and pain, is indeed lord of all wealth."
[Yudhishthira said:] "You are our foremost speaker in this world, bull of the Bharatas; I ask you this; you should tell it to me."
[Bhishma said:] "For one who is parted from sons, wives, pleasures and wealth, and is sunk in hard calamity, steadiness, king, does good.
For one joined with fortitude the body does not waste away; with health of body he gains fortune again.
The king whose men, dear, are established in a sattvic livelihood has steadiness, firmness and resolve in deeds.
Here they cite this ancient tale, again, Yudhishthira, the dialogue of Bali and Vasava.
When the war of gods and asuras was over, the Daityas and Danavas destroyed, the worlds taken by Vishnu's strides, Shatakratu being king of the gods,
the gods being worshipped, the four classes established, the three worlds prospering, the Self-born pleased,
surrounded by Rudras, Vasus, Adityas, the Ashvins and sages, by gandharvas, lords of serpents, siddhas and others, the lord,
once, at the edge of the ocean, in a mountain cave, the wielder of the thunderbolt saw Bali, son of Virochana, and approached him.
Seeing Indra, lord of the gods, seated on Airavata's head, surrounded by hosts of gods, the Daitya lord neither grieved nor trembled.
Seeing Bali standing unchanged and fearless, Shatakratu, mounted on the best of elephants, said:

Daitya, you do not tremble, whether from courage, service to the elders or being formed by austerity; in every way this is very hard.

As he spoke these and other harsh words, insulting him, hearing it, Bali, son of Virochana, unperturbed, said:

When I am held down, Shakra, what use is your boasting? I see you standing with the thunderbolt raised, Purandara.

mahabharata:12:220.34	If the doer were a doer, he would never be made; but because the doer is made, the doer too is without mastery.
